questions.question: What's the difference between unit and integration tests in Rails?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Tests
questions.direct_answer: Unit tests check one piece in isolation (a method, a model's validation): `UserTest` asserts `User.new(name: '').valid?` is false — fast, no DB/HTTP, pinpoint failures. Integration tests check multiple parts working together: a request spec hits `post '/users', params: ...` and asserts the DB changed and the response is 302 — slower (full stack: routing, controller, model, DB, views) but catches wiring bugs unit tests miss. Rails layers: model tests (unit), controller/request tests (integration), system tests (full browser, JS). Pyramid: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration, very few system (slow). Unit tests tell you WHAT broke precisely; integration tests tell you the WIRING works. Both matter: unit for fast feedback on logic, integration for confidence the pieces connect. Don't write only integration (slow, hard to localize) or only unit (misses wiring); balance them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know unit tests check one piece in isolation (fast, pinpoint), integration tests check parts together (slow, catches wiring), and you balance the pyramid.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only integration tests (slow, hard to localize) or only unit (misses wiring bugs) — balance the pyramid.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Unit = one piece in isolation (fast, pinpoint). Integration = parts together (routing+controller+model+DB, catches wiring). Balance the pyramid.

sections.title: Unit vs Integration
sections.content:
unit = one piece in isolation (fast, pinpoint). integration = parts together (routing+controller+model+DB, catches wiring). Balance pyramid.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  S[System tests: few, slow, browser] --> I[Integration tests: fewer]
  I --> U[Unit tests: many, fast, isolated]
```

sections.title: Unit vs integration
sections.content:
```ruby
# UNIT test: one piece in isolation (fast, no DB/HTTP)
# test/models/user_test.rb (Minitest)
class UserTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test 'invalid without a name' do
    user = User.new(name: '')
    refute user.valid?                     # just the validation logic
    assert_equal ["can't be blank"], user.errors[:name]
  end
end
# spec/models/user_spec.rb (RSpec)
RSpec.describe User, type: :model do
  it 'is invalid without a name' do
    expect(User.new(name: '')).not_to be_valid
  end
end
# Fast; pinpoint: tells you the validation logic broke.

# INTEGRATION test: parts together (routing -> controller -> model -> DB -> view)
# spec/requests/users_spec.rb (request spec)
RSpec.describe 'Users', type: :request do
  it 'creates a user' do
    post '/users', params: { user: { name: 'Al' } }
    expect(response).to have_http_status(:found)   # 302 redirect
    expect(User.count).to eq(1)                    # DB changed
    expect(User.last.name).to eq('Al')
  end
end
# test/system/users_test.rb (system test: full browser, JS)
class UsersTest < ActionDispatch::SystemTestCase
  test 'create via form' do
    visit '/users/new'
    fill_in 'Name', with: 'Al'
    click_on 'Create'
    assert_text 'Al'
  end
end

# Rails layers:    model (unit) -> request (integration) -> system (full browser/JS)
# Pyramid:         many unit (fast) / fewer integration / very few system (slow).
# Unit tests    -> what broke precisely (logic).
# Integration  -> the wiring works (parts connect).
# System       -> the user flow works in a real browser (incl. JS).
# Balance: don't write ONLY integration (slow, hard to localize) or ONLY unit (misses wiring).
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Only integration tests (slow, hard to localize failures).
Only unit tests (misses wiring bugs between controller/model/DB).
System tests for pure logic (slow; use unit).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Unit tests check one piece in isolation (a method, a model's validation) — fast, pinpoint failures.
Integration tests check parts together (routing, controller, model, DB, view) — slower, catches wiring.
Rails layers: model (unit) -> request (integration) -> system (full browser, JS).
Pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration, very few system (slow).
Unit tells you WHAT broke; integration tells you the WIRING works. Balance them.
